Understanding Ethereum "Smart Contracts"

To understand the latest Blockchain developments such as running distributed contracts in Ethereum, my game might help you understand the concepts on a practical/tangible level using familiar concepts and analogies.

The "War Tribunal" is a DAPP which takes inputs from all users meeting a certain criteria, executes specified codes based on their inputs, and produces output. In this case, the "War Tribunal" is like a voting booth that only members of a certain game world can enter, who can then vote on elements of a character's game stats. The consensus of that group produces an output which best meets group wishes, all done without an intermediary which always involves some level of opacity.

So here is a DAPP which is operated on a small committee consensus: The "War Tribunal".

A player, Ann, in my game decides she wants to make a new uniform for her soldiers, so she goes to the playing card creation tool, uploads her painting, then uses the tool to copy the stats, abilities & description of her old soldier playing card.

Before the group will allow her new playing card in their game, they will need to review it, and by consensus decide if it should be allowed. The card could be too powerful, or the style of the art doesn't fit their game preferences, etc.

So the player submits her new soldier card to the "Warrior Forge" which is a simple distributed contract which allows anyone with an Ethereum wallet a tool to submit artwork and character specifications/stats. The smart contract makes sure all the inputs meet the requirements, then stores the data on the Blockchain, attributed innately to her ownership. Because the tool is open source, Ann is able to trust the Smart Contract to process her data in an expected/agreed upon way. The crucial element of trust here is that this Smart Contract preserves Ann's "ownership" of the output, meaning Ann is still the only one with keys to unlock the Trading Card, even though this "3rd Party" processed it.

So now that Ann has submitted her new soldier to the "Warrior Forge" smart contract, her Warrior is now an object on the Ethereum Blockchain which only she has the keys to manipulate. Anns new soldier is now available to the game engine, but the Smart Contract [Warrior Forge] has one more job - it presents Ann's new soldier to the War Tribunal. At this time, Ann has a choice - she can keep the card registered as her sole property and with whatever stats she gave it, but the game world may have many matches which she would be prohibited from playing that card. Instead, if she hands over ownership of the card to the "War Tribunal" [which remember is a committee based Smart Contract] - they can vote on things like its art style and its stats and depending on their consensus, the soldier could be classified 'Modern Era' due to the uniform, or 'OP' due to an ability. The "War Tribunal" DAPP then stores the newly revised Soldier Trading Card on the blockchain. But because Ann submitted it to the "War Tribunal", depending on the rules of their Realm and the Artists wishes, a certain number of "copies"(1) of this card will become available. Ann will get her copy, which remains under her control with her keys.

1) It's not really a copy, it is only stored once, but new cryptographic tokens are created which will allow a certain number of additional users to make use of the asset. In other words, Ann's card now becomes 20 playable cards that can be sold or traded in the game. The reason for not simply creating 20 copies of the Soldier is that storing things on the Blockchain is expensive so you only store the absolute minimum to do the job.

They began to work out songs early in 1969, and in February and March the group was in London at Morgan Studios, preparing for the beginnings of basic tracks for their album, although the first few almost finished songs didn't show up until they were at Olympic Studios in April and May under the direction of producer Jimmy Miller. The music community was already aware of the linkup, despite Clapton's claim that he was cutting an album of his own on which Winwood would play. The promoters and record companies got involved, pushing those concerned for an album and a tour.

The album cover was a photo of a young girl with no clothes on holding a model spaceship. According to photographer Bob Seidemann, who shot the cover, he had the idea but did not have someone to pose. While riding the London subway, he saw a young girl who would be perfect and asked her to pose for the cover. He went to the girl's house to ask her parents' permission to pose topless for the cover. They agreed, but the girl backed out. However, the girl's younger sister begged the parents to let her pose instead. They agreed and the younger sister ended up posing for the cover. Bob Seidemann came up with the concept and took the photo, which represents humankind's relationship with technology (this was when the mission to put a man on the moon was big news). The band wasn't yet named, and when Seidemann took the photo, he called it "Blind Faith." Clapton decided that should be the name of the band.

Steve Winwood – keyboards, vocals, guitars; bass guitar Eric Clapton – guitars Ric Grech – bass guitar, violin Ginger Baker – drums, percussion
